Its decline is often traced to failed date-setting (e.g. Millerism in 1844) and to the rise of futurism and critical scholarship.

Futurists point to Irenaeus and Hippolytus, who expected a future personal Antichrist and a literal three-and-a-half-year tribulation. Systematic futurism was developed by the Jesuit Francisco Ribera (c. 1590) and Cardinal Bellarmine, partly in answer to Protestant historicism. Protestant writers (S. R. Maitland, J. H. Todd, Darby) revived it in the nineteenth century, and it is now the most widespread popular-level reading.

Historicist critics have used Ribera's Jesuit role polemically. Futurists respond that their view stands or falls on exegesis, and they claim the early fathers' expectation of a future Antichrist as precedent.

The spiritual or symbolic reading of Revelation goes back to the Alexandrian tradition (Origen) and above all to Tyconius and Augustine. Their non-chronological, recapitulating reading of the Apocalypse governed much of the medieval church. Modern idealism was articulated by William Milligan (1886) and popularised in Reformed circles by Hendriksen.
Idealism as a named 'school' is a modern category. Its patristic roots are shared with amillennialism.

The eclectic approach is a late twentieth-century development in evangelical scholarship, best represented by G. K. Beale's 1999 commentary and followed by others such as Grant Osborne and Craig Keener. It deliberately combines the idealist core with preterist attention to the first-century setting and a futurist consummation, and so draws on every older stream of interpretation.
Proponents note that patristic commentators already mixed historical, symbolic and future readings, so eclecticism is arguably older than its label.

The thousand years symbolise the fullness of Christ's reign now (ten cubed: completeness). It began when the Lamb who was slain took the throne, and believers reign with him as those seated with Christ in the heavenly places. It is not a future earthly era to wait for but the present reality of the kingdom.

Proponents stress the believer's present reign in Christ more than the heavenly reign of departed saints. Those who expect the gospel's growing triumph also lean toward the present-progressive stance.

The accuser was cast down and bound by the cross: Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them, and the strong man is bound so his house can be plundered. Satan's power now is chiefly deception, a lie about identity, which loses its hold where the truth of Christ is seen.
Revelation 12 (the accuser thrown down) and Revelation 20 (the dragon bound) are read as two pictures of the cross's victory.
The first resurrection is the new birth: being raised with Christ from spiritual death into union with him. Those who share in it reign with him now, and over them 'the second death has no power'.

Christ's appearing will consummate what the cross accomplished, bringing the resurrection, the judgment and the fullness of the new creation together. The view emphasises that Christ already 'comes' to his people by the Spirit, and that the final appearing completes a victory already won rather than starting one.

Many 'coming' texts (for example the clouds of Revelation 1:7, or the 'coming' to churches in Revelation 2–3) are read as present or first-century comings in judgment and grace. A minority within the broader movement leans toward fully realised readings, which most proponents reject.

The view rejects a separate escape from a future tribulation as a fear-based framework. Believers are already 'caught up' in the sense of being seated with Christ, and they will be gathered to him at his one appearing.
Proponents give the question little weight: the believer's security rests on union with Christ, not on a timetable.

The 'great tribulation' of the Olivet Discourse fell on the old covenant order in the Jewish War and the destruction of the temple in AD 70. In Revelation, tribulation is also the ongoing experience of believers who share in Christ's suffering and kingdom (Revelation 1:9), and they overcome it by the blood of the Lamb, not by fear.

Preterist-leaning proponents tie the tribulation to AD 66-70; idealist-leaning proponents treat it as a pattern throughout the age. Almost all reject a future seven-year tribulation as the book's centre.

'Antichrist' is above all a spirit and a mindset: whatever denies that Christ has come in the flesh and puts something in his place. The beasts picture the power of the flesh, persecuting rule and false religion. The mark on the hand and forehead is a life and mind shaped by fear and self-effort, set against the Father's name on the forehead.
Many accept a first-century referent (Nero, the persecuting empire) as the first layer of the symbol, and read 666 as the number of humanity, falling short of God's seventh-day rest.

'This generation' meant Jesus' hearers: the shaking of the old covenant world and the temple's fall were fulfilled by AD 70, making way for the new covenant kingdom that cannot be shaken. The final consummation remains Christ's to bring.
Some proponents read the whole discourse in idealist terms instead (contemporaries-dual).

Daniel's seventy weeks are fulfilled in Christ: he finished transgression, made an end of sin, brought in everlasting righteousness and confirmed the new covenant by his death. The seventieth week is about the Messiah, not a future Antichrist.

The date is secondary because the unveiling of Christ speaks to every generation. Proponents with a covenantal emphasis tend to favour an early (pre-70) date. The date of Revelation is disputed among scholars.
Preterist-leaning proponents favour the early date; others are content with c. AD 95.

The true Israel, the Bride and the New Jerusalem are the one people of God, Jew and Gentile, in union with Christ. The 144,000 (twelve times twelve times a thousand) and the innumerable multitude are two views of the same complete people.
Some proponents also expect many Jewish people to come to faith in Christ, without a separate national programme.

Because the decisive battle is already won, the church reads history from victory: the Rider on the white horse conquers by his word, and the harvest of Revelation 14 is the fruit of the gospel. The leaven of the kingdom is expected to work through the whole lump.
Proponents are uniformly hopeful and anti-fear, but some hold the amillennial 'realistic' expectation that wheat and tares grow together until the end.

The kingdom is present now, within and among believers, as Christ reigns from the throne and his people reign in life through grace. It grows as minds are renewed and the gospel spreads, and it is consummated in the new heavens and new earth.
Amillennial-leaning proponents place the emphasis on inaugurated-consummated (already/not yet) rather than progressive growth.

Judgment centres on the cross, where the world's sin was judged and the ruler of this world cast out. A final judgment at Christ's appearing completes it, with the books opened and death and Hades themselves thrown into the lake of fire.

Within the view the lake of fire is read in different ways: as eternal judgment, as the final destruction of all that opposes life, or as purifying fire. Proponents present it with care rather than as a tool of fear.

The view's roots lie in the spiritual exegesis of Alexandria, Tyconius and Augustine, whose present-reign, two-cities reading of Revelation dominated the church for a millennium. Its distinctive modern form, emphasising the finished work, union with Christ and the renewed mind, has grown since the late twentieth century.
No stance fits exactly: the Augustinian stream supplies the view's historical weight, but its modern finished-work form is recent.
The Thousand Years

An angel binds Satan for a thousand years so that he can no longer deceive the nations; enthroned souls “came to life” (ezēsan) and reign with Christ in the “first resurrection”; afterwards Satan is released, gathers Gog and Magog, and is cast into the lake of fire. The only passage in Scripture that names a thousand-year period, it gives the millennial views their names.

Does Revelation 20 follow the return of Christ in Revelation 19 chronologically (premillennial), or does it recapitulate and describe the whole period between the two advents (amillennial and most postmillennial readings)? Closely tied are what “bound” means (compare Matthew 12:29, where Jesus binds the strong man), whether ezēsan in 20:4 and 20:5 must mean bodily resurrection both times, and whether “thousand” is literal or symbolic.

The thousand years is the long, symbolically numbered gospel age, begun at Christ's first advent and enthronement. Satan is bound so he cannot stop the gospel from discipling the nations (20:3), and the age moves, through the Spirit's work, toward a historical flourishing of the faith before a brief final rebellion (20:7-9) and Christ's return. Warfield read the reigning souls as the saints in heaven (the intermediate state); Gentry and Boettner stress the gradual triumph of the kingdom on earth that the binding makes possible.

The binding language echoes Jesus' own claim to have bound the strong man (Matthew 12:29) and to see Satan fall (Luke 10:18; John 12:31-32), and the stated purpose of the binding is specifically about the nations, which matches the Great Commission. “Thousand” is used elsewhere for a vast, complete number (Psalm 50:10; Deuteronomy 7:9). Postmillennialists add that other texts (Psalm 110, 1 Corinthians 15:25, Matthew 13:31-33) predict growing dominion, so the millennium is naturally that era of growth.

Premillennialists reply that Satan is still described as active, prowling and deceiving in the New Testament (1 Peter 5:8; 2 Corinthians 4:4), and the abyss is sealed over him, which they think is far stronger than restriction. Amillennialists, who share the recapitulation reading, object that Revelation 20 itself says nothing about a future golden age within history; the visible reign is in heaven, and the age ends in global apostasy (20:8).

Revelation 20:1 begins a new vision that goes back to the first advent, as Revelation 12 does. The thousand years is the whole church age. Satan's binding is his restraint from stopping the gospel among the nations or gathering them for the final battle before the appointed time. The “first resurrection” is either regeneration (Augustine) or, more often today, the believer's entrance into heavenly life with Christ at death (Hoekema, Kline, Riddlebarger, Storms); the second, bodily resurrection comes at Christ's single return, followed by the final judgment.

The final battle of 20:8 is described with the same Ezekiel 38-39 imagery and the same article (“the war”) as 16:14 and 19:19, which suggests it is the same event seen again. The thrones of 20:4 are in heaven, as elsewhere in Revelation, and the persons are “souls”. John 5:24-29 has the same pattern of a spiritual resurrection now and a bodily one at the end. The rest of the New Testament teaches one return, one general resurrection and one judgment (John 5:28-29; Acts 24:15; Matthew 25:31-46).

Since Henry Alford, premillennialists have pressed that ezēsan cannot mean spiritual life in 20:4 and bodily life in 20:5 within the same passage, and that the word anastasis almost always means bodily resurrection. They also argue that 19:20 and 20:10 link the two chapters in sequence: the beast and false prophet are already in the lake of fire when the devil joins them.

The visions run in order: Christ returns (19:11-21), Satan is then bound, and the martyrs and faithful are bodily raised to reign with Christ on earth for a long period (whether exactly a thousand years or not). After the rebellion at the end of that period come the resurrection of the rest of the dead and the final judgment. This is the hope of early church writers such as Papias, Justin and Irenaeus, held without the dispensational distinction between Israel and the church.

The plain sequence of the narrative and the parallel use of ezēsan: if the second “came to life” (20:5) is bodily, so is the first. 1 Corinthians 15:23-24 seems to allow an interval between the resurrection of “those who belong to Christ” and “the end”. The interpretation is also old: Justin (Dialogue 80-81) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies V) held an earthly kingdom after Christ's return.

Amillennialists and postmillennialists answer that Revelation is a series of parallel visions rather than a single timeline, and 20:1 starts a fresh vision. They also ask why, if Christ has returned and the nations have been destroyed (19:18-21), there are still nations to deceive in 20:3 and 20:8, and why no other New Testament text clearly teaches two bodily resurrections separated by an age.

The thousand years is a literal future era after the Second Coming in which Christ reigns from Jerusalem on David's throne. In that era God fulfils his unconditional covenant promises to national Israel (land, kingdom, temple), and the raptured church reigns with him. The binding is a complete removal of Satan's activity from the earth. The first resurrection happens in stages (Christ, the raptured church, tribulation martyrs, Old Testament saints), and the rest of the dead are raised to the great white throne judgment afterwards.

Six repetitions of “a thousand years” in a few verses suggest a real duration. The binding is described in heavy terms (seized, bound, thrown into the abyss, shut and sealed), which does not fit Satan's current activity. The reading also fits a consistent literal hermeneutic that expects the Old Testament kingdom prophecies (Isaiah 2; 11; 65; Zechariah 14) to be fulfilled on earth, in history, for Israel.

Critics observe that numbers in Revelation are overwhelmingly symbolic (seven spirits, 144,000, 666), and that Revelation 20 itself says nothing about Israel, Jerusalem's temple, or the land. They argue that importing those elements from the prophets presupposes the dispensational system rather than deriving it from this text.

Partial preterists (usually postmillennial, as Gentry, or amillennial, as some others) read Revelation 4-19 as chiefly fulfilled in the first-century judgment on Jerusalem and the persecuting Roman beast, and see Revelation 20 as looking beyond that to the long era of Christ's reign that began with his first coming. The martyrs under Nero are vindicated and reign; the binding began with Christ's ministry and cross; the final release of Satan and the end are still future.

Revelation's repeated time indicators (“soon”, “the time is near”, 1:1, 1:3, 22:6, 22:10) govern the bulk of the prophecy, while Revelation 20 explicitly introduces a long period (a thousand years), which marks it off from the near events. The martyr language in 20:4 (beheaded for the testimony of Jesus, not worshipping the beast) ties it to the persecutions earlier in the book.

Futurists challenge the early (pre-70) dating of Revelation that the preterist frame usually relies on; most scholars favour c. AD 95 on the basis of Irenaeus (the date is disputed). Full preterists, from the other side, argue it is inconsistent to apply “soon” to Revelation 1-19 and then put the resurrection and judgment of 20:11-15 thousands of years later.

All of Revelation, including chapter 20, was fulfilled by the AD 70 destruction of Jerusalem. Many full preterists take the thousand years as the transitional generation between the cross and AD 70 (or a symbolic era closing then). The first resurrection is the new life of believers in Christ, and the judgment and emptying of Hades (20:13-14) took place at the parousia in AD 70. There is no future bodily resurrection or end of history.

Proponents appeal to the time statements in the frame of the book (1:1-3; 22:6-12, “do not seal up the prophecy... the time is near”), and to Daniel 12:2 and 12:7, which they say tie the resurrection to the shattering of the holy people's power. They argue that their view applies “near” consistently to the whole book.

Critics, including partial preterists, note that this view denies a future bodily resurrection and visible Second Coming, which all the ecumenical creeds confess (the Nicene Creed: he “will come again... to judge the living and the dead”), and so stands outside historic orthodoxy. They also argue it has to compress a “thousand years” into roughly forty. Proponents answer that Scripture outranks creeds and that the creeds did not anticipate the time-statement argument.

Historicists read Revelation as a continuous prophecy of church history from John's day to the end, with Revelation 20 coming after the fall of the papal “beast” and Antichrist. Many historicists (Elliott) were premillennial and placed the thousand years after a future return; others (Barnes, and much of the Puritan and post-Reformation tradition) expected a future era of gospel triumph after the overthrow of papal Rome, before Christ returns.

The book's numbered sequences (seals, trumpets, bowls) look like a progressive history, and the year-day principle (Numbers 14:34; Ezekiel 4:6) allows long historical periods. To historicists, the record of church history read alongside the chapters confirms the scheme.

Critics point out that historicist identifications have changed with each generation and have often set dates that failed. The scheme also tends to centre Western European history in a way that John's first readers could not have understood.

Revelation presents recurring spiritual realities rather than datable events. Following Hendriksen's “progressive parallelism”, chapter 20 is the last of seven parallel sections, each covering the age from the first to the second advent. The binding says Satan cannot halt the gathering of the nations through the gospel; the reigning souls depict the present victory of the faithful dead; Gog and Magog depict the final, intensified opposition that the church must always expect.

Revelation's genre is apocalyptic, full of symbols, and it is addressed to seven real churches that needed comfort for their own day and every day. The cycles of judgment in the book visibly repeat and end in the final judgment more than once (6:12-17; 11:15-18; 16:17-21; 19:11-21; 20:11-15).

Critics say that idealism risks detaching the visions from any real history, although Revelation claims to show “what must soon take place” and predicts a concrete return, resurrection and judgment. Most idealists answer that they affirm those final events and read only the intervening symbols as transhistorical.
The Olivet Discourse (Matthew)

After Jesus predicts the temple's destruction, the disciples ask when it will happen and what will be the sign of his coming (parousia) and of the end of the age (synteleia tou aiōnos). Jesus describes false messiahs, wars, persecution, the gospel going to the whole world, the “abomination of desolation”, great tribulation, cosmic signs and the Son of Man coming on the clouds. He then says “this generation” (hē genea hautē) will not pass away until all these things take place (24:34), but that no one knows the day or hour (24:36).

What “this generation” (genea) in 24:34 means, and whether the discourse moves at 24:36 from the AD 70 destruction to the final coming. Nearly every reading depends on how the timing word in 24:34 relates to the coming of the Son of Man in 24:30 (quoting Daniel 7:13) and to the parousia language in 24:27, 37 and 39.

Matthew 24:4-34 predicts the events of AD 66-70. “This generation” means Jesus' contemporaries, as it does every other time in Matthew (11:16; 12:41-45; 23:36). The abomination of desolation is the Roman (and Zealot) desecration of the temple; the great tribulation is the siege of Jerusalem; and the Son of Man “coming on the clouds” (24:30) is Daniel 7:13 imagery for Christ's vindication and enthronement, shown in judgment on the city. Most partial preterists (Gentry, Sproul, DeMar, France) see a shift at 24:36 to the still-future final coming.

The disciples' question is set off by the temple prediction (24:1-3). Within Matthew the timing is tied together: 23:36 says judgment will fall on “this generation”, 16:28 says some standing there will not taste death, and 26:64 says the high priest will “see” the Son of Man coming. In the prophets, cosmic collapse is standard imagery for the fall of nations (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4), and the details of the siege recorded by Josephus closely fit.

Futurists reply that Jesus describes the coming as universal and visible, like lightning (24:27), followed by a worldwide gathering of the elect (24:31), and that the tribulation is called unequalled in all history (24:21). The contrast between “these things” and “that day” is also disputed, since parousia appears on both sides of 24:36 (24:27, 37, 39).

Most modern postmillennialists hold the partial-preterist reading of 24:1-34 and stress what it means for history. The great tribulation is behind the church, not ahead of it. The gospel was preached to the whole oikoumenē before AD 70 (24:14; compare Colossians 1:6, 23), and the end of the old covenant order leaves the kingdom free to grow. Kik divided the discourse at 24:35/36: the first part is AD 70, the second the unannounced Second Coming at the end of history.

Paul uses the same language of universal proclamation about his own day (Romans 1:8; 10:18; Colossians 1:23). Removing a future global tribulation takes away the main textual objection to an optimistic view of the church age, and 24:36-51 still teaches watchfulness for a future coming.

Amillennialists and premillennialists argue that the signs (deception, lawlessness, persecution) are presented as typical of the whole age until the end, so the discourse does not support optimism even if AD 70 is in view. Futurists add that 24:14 ties the gospel's spread to “the end” (to telos), not to the temple's fall.

The discourse answers both questions together. AD 70 is a real, near fulfilment and also a type of the final judgment, so the signs are both fulfilled in the first century and repeated through the whole age. The tribulation, deception and false Christs mark the entire interadvental period and intensify before the end. Amillennialists differ on details: Hoekema treats the signs as present throughout history; Riddlebarger accepts a preterist reading of much of 24:4-34 while holding 24:29-31 and 36-51 as future.

Prophetic “foreshortening” is common in the Old Testament: Isaiah speaks of the return from Babylon and the messianic age in one breath. The disciples assumed the temple's fall meant the end of the age, and Jesus answers both without separating them sharply, while still saying the end is not yet (24:6).

Preterists object that “all these things” in 24:34 forbids double reference: the whole set of signs must occur within the generation. Dispensationalists object that a vague, age-long tribulation empties the specific language of 24:15-21 (a single event, a specific place, a flight from Judea).

Jesus looks at two events through one lens: the near destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the age, with the second still future. The tribulation of 24:21-29 culminates at the end in a final crisis, which the church will go through. The coming of 24:30-31 is the single posttribulational return, when the angels gather the elect with a trumpet (the same gathering as 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). On 24:34, writers such as Blomberg take “all these things” to mean the preliminary signs of 24:4-28, all of which had begun before AD 70, while the coming itself is open-ended.

The return comes “immediately after” the tribulation (24:29), and the elect are gathered then (24:31), not before, which fits a posttribulational return. Luke's parallel clarifies that a long Gentile period follows the fall of Jerusalem (Luke 21:24). The “trumpet” and “gathering” match Paul's rapture language.

Preterists ask how “all these things” in 24:33-34 can exclude the coming in 24:30, which is the climax of the list. Dispensationalists argue that the setting is Jewish (Judea, the Sabbath, 24:16, 20) and concerns Israel, not the church.

Most of the discourse describes the future seven-year tribulation, especially its second half (24:15-28), which begins when the Antichrist sets up the abomination in a rebuilt temple (Daniel 9:27; 2 Thessalonians 2:4). The passage addresses believing Israel in that period, not the church, which will already have been raptured. “This generation” means the generation alive when these signs begin (Walvoord, Ice), or alternatively “this race” of Israel (Scofield). The Son of Man's coming in 24:30 is the visible Second Coming to set up the millennial kingdom.

Jesus himself links the abomination to Daniel (24:15), which dispensationalists place in the future seventieth week. The scale of the tribulation (“such as has not been from the beginning of the world”, 24:21) and the cosmic signs exceed AD 70. The surrounding parables (24:32-33, the fig tree) describe the generation that “sees all these things”.

Critics argue that genea elsewhere in Matthew always means Jesus' contemporaries, and that the reading “the generation that sees these signs” is not natural Greek usage. Luke's parallel (Luke 21:20) interprets the abomination as Jerusalem surrounded by armies, which points to AD 70. Pre-tribulational placement of the church outside the discourse is also contested by historic premillennialists.

The whole discourse, including 24:36-51, was fulfilled within the generation that heard it. There is one question, one coming and one end of the age (the end of the old covenant age), and “this generation” governs all of it. The parousia, the gathering of the elect and the end of the age took place in AD 70, so no future visible return remains.

Full preterists stress that the disciples' question is a single question with linked parts (24:3), that “all these things” (24:34) includes the coming of 24:30, and that parousia is used both before and after 24:36. They argue that dividing the discourse at 24:36 is an inconsistency on the part of partial preterists.

Partial preterists and futurists answer that 24:36 begins a contrast (peri de, “but concerning”) between datable signs and an unannounced day. They also point to other texts that present the return as bodily and visible (Acts 1:11) and that tie it to the general resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:23). Critics also note that this view sits outside the creedal confession of a future return to judge the living and the dead.
The Olivet Discourse (Mark)

Mark's shorter version, probably the earliest. The disciples ask only when the temple will be destroyed and what the sign will be that “all these things” are about to be accomplished (13:4). Jesus warns of deceivers and persecution, says the gospel must first be preached to all nations (13:10), speaks of the abomination “standing where he ought not” (13:14), describes cosmic signs and the Son of Man coming with great power, says this generation will not pass until all these things happen (13:30), and ends with a call to watch because no one knows the day or hour (13:32-37).

Mark's version of the question is only about the temple and “these things”, and there is no parousia language. Preterists take this as evidence that the discourse is about AD 70; futurists see the same structure as Matthew (signs, then a final coming) and take 13:32 as the turning point toward the last day.

Mark's framing (13:1-4) is entirely about the temple, so 13:5-31 describes AD 70. The masculine participle in 13:14 (hestēkota, “he” standing) suggests a person or army desecrating the sanctuary. 13:24-27 uses Isaiah's and Daniel's imagery for the fall of the old order and the Son of Man's vindication, with the “gathering of the elect” referring to the worldwide mission. Many partial preterists see 13:32-37 as moving to the final day.

Without the parousia question that appears in Matthew, the natural antecedent of “these things” in 13:4, 13:29 and 13:30 is the temple's destruction. Jesus' warning to flee to the mountains (13:14) fits Judea under siege and makes little sense for a global end-time event.

Futurists reply that 13:24-27 introduces a decisive, visible coming “with great power and glory” and a gathering “from the ends of the earth”, which goes well beyond AD 70, and that Mark's readers would have heard Daniel 7:13 as a coming at the end. Full preterists object that the break at 13:32 is arbitrary.

Postmillennialists generally share the partial-preterist reading. They emphasise 13:10, which says the gospel must first be preached to all nations before the fall of Jerusalem, and stress that the discourse warns about the first-century crisis rather than predicting the course of the whole church age. Christ's present reign continues after AD 70, and the church's task of discipling the nations goes on.

The emphasis is on local events (Judea, housetops, winter) and the disciples' own persecution before councils and synagogues (13:9), which fits the first century. Acts and Paul's letters describe the gospel reaching the nations within that generation.
Critics say the passage gives no positive picture of the later age at all; postmillennial optimism has to come from other texts. Futurists also question whether 13:10 was fully realised before AD 70.

The discourse mixes near and far horizons. The temple's destruction is a type, a preview, of the final judgment, and the dangers it describes (deception, persecution, false messiahs) continue throughout the age. 13:24-27 points to the Second Coming, and the call to watch (13:33-37) applies to every generation of the church.
The parable of the doorkeeper (13:34-37) addresses “all” (13:37) and assumes a long absence of the master, which suggests that the discourse looks beyond the first generation.
Preterists argue that the same “all” in 13:30 limits the whole set of signs to one generation, so the two horizons cannot be separated as easily as the amillennial reading suggests.

Historic premillennialists read Mark 13 much as Ladd did: Jesus spoke of the fall of Jerusalem and of the end of the age without clearly separating them in time. The near event fulfilled the first horizon, and the final tribulation and posttribulational return still lie ahead. The gathering of the elect (13:27) is the church's resurrection and rapture at the end of the tribulation.
